content.thinking:
I need to be careful here — the impact figures were measured externally, not computed by me, so I should reference them as given data rather than presenting them as my own calculations or offering alternative numbers.

For assumptions, I'll note the leak's origin wasn't identified since no deploys appeared in the searched window, the restart's effectiveness is correlational rather than proven, and the code fix is still an unreviewed draft. The root cause is a memory leak in the service that grows with uptime, with heap climbing steadily while traffic stayed flat, and no deploy changes found to explain it. For the executive summary, I want to avoid technical component names where possible and write it for a non-technical reader.

assumptions: The leak is attributed to code already running before the incident. Change history was only retrieved for roughly the 36 hours before the alert; a change older than that window, or one made outside the recorded deploy/release/flag channels, would not have appeared and cannot be ruled out.

The restart is treated as the remedy because the service returned to baseline shortly after it. This is a correlation observed once, not a proven causal fix, and the underlying leak was not directly instrumented or heap-dumped.
Explicit heap measurements only appear in the logs from 07:13 onward; the earlier portion of the growth curve is taken from the service's memory metric rather than from logged heap values.

The 'ClientDisconnected' account-page errors were already occurring at a similar rate before the onset and are assumed to be pre-existing background noise rather than a symptom of the leak, though the elevated portion during the window is assumed to be caused by the slowdown.

The root cause is inferred from the shape of the data (memory rising while traffic and CPU allocation stayed flat); no code-level confirmation of the leaking allocation was obtained during the incident.
The proposed code change is a draft pull request that was not reviewed, merged, or deployed during the incident, so it is not assumed to have contributed to recovery.
input.executive_summary:
Early on the morning of 28 September 2026, one of the shop's back-end services gradually consumed more and more memory while serving a steady, normal volume of traffic. As memory filled up, the service slowed down and a small additional share of customer requests — mostly on account pages — failed instead of completing. Customers who hit the problem would have seen slow or failed account page loads; the great majority of requests continued to succeed throughout.

The degradation began at 06:57 UTC and the service was back to its normal behaviour by 07:23 UTC, a stretch of roughly 26 minutes. Monitoring raised an alert at 07:22 UTC, once memory use crossed its threshold. The on-call automation investigated, ruled out any recent code, configuration, or feature-flag change, identified the pattern as a memory leak, and restarted the service. It returned to its normal baseline shortly after, and the restart was confirmed as effective at 07:25 UTC. A draft code fix was subsequently opened for review. The impact figures quoted elsewhere in this report were measured from the shop's own traffic over the 06:57–07:23 window.

The restart clears the accumulated memory but does not remove the leak, so the condition is expected to recur as the process runs; the proposed fix still needs review and release.
input.root_cause: A memory leak in io-shop that accumulates with process uptime rather than with load: heap grew steadily and monotonically from about 06:54 onward (logs show it climbing minute over minute toward the 2048MiB limit) while request volume stayed flat and the CPU allocation was unchanged, and p95/p99 latency degraded in lockstep with the heap growth. No deploys, releases, or feature-flag changes were recorded in the windows searched (roughly the preceding 36 hours), so the leak was present in the already-running process and the change that introduced it was not identified.
